rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act rent cap
rules.requirement: An owner may not raise the gross rental rate over any 12-month period by more than 5 percent plus the local percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, and may not raise rent more than twice in 12 months for the same tenant. New tenancies (no prior tenant remaining) may start at any rate, and the cap applies only to later increases.
rules.key_value: 5% + CPI, max 10%
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential real property (dwellings and units intended for human habitation, including units in mobilehome parks) that has had a certificate of occupancy for more than 15 years and is not otherwise exempt.
rules.exemptions: Exempt: deed-restricted/subsidized affordable housing; school and university dormitories; housing under a stricter local rent control; housing with a certificate of occupancy within the last 15 years; separately alienable homes/condos owned by non-corporate, non-REIT owners with written exemption notice; owner-occupied duplexes; homeowners of mobilehomes.
rules.interaction: Does not expand or limit local governments' authority to adopt rent controls consistent with Civ. Code ch. 2.7 (§ 1954.50 et seq.), and housing under a local rent control that restricts annual increases to less than the state cap is exempt. Rent increase notice must be given under Civ. Code § 827. Statute exempts housing under stricter local rent control; yields to local California rent-cap ordinances.
rules.quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower,

supporting_sources.quoted_span: rent increases are limited to no more than 5% plus the percentage change in the cost of living for the region in which the property is located, or 10% whichever is lower).

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act just cause
rules.requirement: After a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months, the owner may terminate the tenancy only for stated at-fault or no-fault just cause. For no-fault terminations the owner must pay one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days of notice or waive the final month's rent.
rules.key_value: Just cause after 12 months' occupancy; no-fault relocation = one month's rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental dwellings in California where the tenant has occupied the unit continuously and lawfully for 12 months (or 24 months if adult tenants were added), unless exempt or covered by a local just-cause ordinance.
rules.exemptions: Exempts transient/hotel occupancy, certain institutional housing and dormitories, shared-facility owner residences, single-family owner-occupied residences (renting up to two units or bedrooms), owner-occupied duplexes, housing with a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, separately alienable property with a non-corporate owner and written exemption notice, deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing, and property covered by a qualifying local just-cause ordinance.
rules.interaction: Does not apply where a local just-cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, or a more protective local ordinance, governs the property; a property cannot be subject to both. Relocation assistance is credited against any other relocation assistance required by other law. Does not apply where local just-cause ordinances govern.
rules.quoted_span: after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.

rules.title: California security deposit cap and return rules
rules.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security exceeding one month's rent (two months' rent for small natural-person landlords owning no more than two properties with four units total, except when the tenant is a service member), and must return the deposit with an itemized statement within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates. Security cannot be labeled nonrefundable, and bad-faith retention can bring statutory damages of up to twice the deposit.
rules.key_value: One month's rent cap (two months for small landlords); 21-day return deadline
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to security for any rental agreement for residential property used as the tenant's dwelling in California.
rules.exemptions: The one-month cap does not apply to security collected before July 1, 2024; it does not bar advance payment of six or more months' rent for a lease of six months or longer, or agreed fee-based alterations at the tenant's request.
rules.quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.

supporting_sources.quoted_span: Starting July 1, 2024, many landlords may only charge one month's rent for unfurnished and furnished units

rules.title: California application screening fee limits
rules.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket costs and the reasonable value of time spent, never more than $30 per applicant (adjustable annually with CPI since 1998), and may not charge it when no unit is or will soon be available. The landlord must either consider applications in order and approve the first qualified applicant (charging only when an application is actually considered), or refund the full fee within 7 days of selecting a tenant or 30 days of application, whichever is first; an itemized receipt is required.
rules.key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted; itemized receipt required
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any landlord (owner of residential rental property) or their agent who charges an applicant a screening fee for a residential rental.
rules.interaction: Applies notwithstanding Civ. Code § 1950.5, and the fee is not treated as security under that section. It does not preempt rules on deposits and fees under federal or state housing assistance programs.
rules.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.

supporting_sources.quoted_span: The landlord cannot charge a prospective tenant a screening fee if no rental unit is actually available.

rules.title: California FEHA housing screening limits
rules.requirement: Owners may not discriminate against or harass a person because of source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers and other public assistance). Where a government rent subsidy applies, income standards must be based on the tenant's share of rent, and applicants must be allowed to offer alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history; owners may still ask about the level or source of income.
rules.key_value: Source of income protected; subsidy-based income test uses tenant's portion of rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to owners of any housing accommodation in California, with no stated size, age or owner-type limits.
rules.citation: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA); Cal. Gov. Code § 12955
rules.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income,

supporting_sources.citation_as_extracted: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
supporting_sources.quoted_span: California law protects tenants from discrimination based on how a tenant will be paying rent (“source of income”).

supporting_sources.citation_as_extracted: California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA)
supporting_sources.quoted_span: Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.

rules.title: California common pricing algorithm ban
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm, meaning software or other technology used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, set or influence a price, as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade, or to coerce another person to adopt the algorithm's recommended price or term. The text is general and does not name rental housing.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person using or distributing a common pricing algorithm in California; the text does not limit it to residential rentals or specific building types.
rules.exemptions: The end consumer of a product or service is excluded from the definition of 'person'.
rules.interaction: Section 16729(c) states that nothing in the section impairs or limits the applicability of antitrust laws. Statute does not limit antitrust laws; nothing about local rules.
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

rules.title: NJ no state rent control; municipalities may adopt rent control
rules.requirement: The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents, but municipalities may pass rent control or rent leveling ordinances enforced by local boards. Landlords may raise rent only by proper lease termination and written notice, the increase must not be unconscionable, and it must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion of construction.
rules.key_value: No state cap; local rent control permitted; new multiple dwellings exempt 30 years
rules.coverage_conditions: Statewide rent increase notice and unconscionability rules apply to residential rentals generally; whether a unit is subject to a rent cap depends on the municipality's rent control ordinance.
rules.exemptions: Newly constructed multiple dwellings are exempt from local rent control for 30 years after completion; governmentally subsidized rents, HUD-owned or subsidized developments, and NJHMFA-financed projects may be exempt from local rent control ordinances.
rules.interaction: State law sets no rent cap and leaves rent control to municipal ordinances; rent increases must comply with any municipal ordinance, and the Newly Constructed Multiple Dwellings Law exempts new buildings from local rent control for 30 years. State sets no cap and delegates rent control to municipalities; delegation, not yielding.
rules.quoted_span:
The State of New Jersey has no laws that establish, govern or control rents. Municipalities 
may pass an ordinance establishing rent control or rent leveling.

rules.title: NJ Anti-Eviction Act
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may remove a tenant or refuse to renew a lease only for a statutory good cause and through a court judgment for possession. Each cause except nonpayment requires a written Notice to Quit with a cause-specific period (3 days to 3 years), some causes need a prior Notice to Cease, and removal for substantial health and safety violations requires relocation assistance first.
rules.key_value: Good cause required; Notice to Quit periods from 3 days up to 3 years depending on cause; relocation assistance of 6 times monthly rent for illegal occupancy evictions
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties, including single-family homes, mobile homes and mobile home park land, apartment buildings and complexes, and rooming and boarding houses.
rules.exemptions: Not applicable to two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units, hotel/motel/guest-house transient or seasonal guests (unless the occupant has no alternate residence and resides there continually), or a unit held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies it.
rules.interaction: Rent increases underlying a nonpayment-of-increase eviction must comply with other laws and municipal ordinances, including rent control. Condominium/cooperative conversion evictions must also comply with the conversion regulations and the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act.
rules.quoted_span:
No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a 
lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

supporting_sources.quoted_span:
Tenants of landlord-occupied two- and three-family dwellings can be removed only when 
a court issues an order for eviction.

rules.title: NJ Security Deposit Law
rules.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent held as security, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, and a pet deposit cannot push the total above the cap.
rules.key_value: 1.5 x monthly rent; annual increase max 10% of current deposit
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to most residential rental properties in New Jersey, including mobile homes.
rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied two- or three-family dwellings are exempt, but a tenant there can make the law apply by sending the landlord a written request, effective 30 days later.
rules.quoted_span:
The maximum-security deposit to be collected by the landlord cannot be more than 
one and one-half times one month’s rent ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 ).

supporting_sources.quoted_span:
Within 30 days after the termination of a tenancy, a landlord must return the security 
deposit, plus interest earned less deductions, to the tenant ( N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1).

rules.title: NJ rental application fee cap
rules.requirement: A landlord or agent may not require an application or similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property that exceeds $50, adjusted annually for CPI increases. Violators face penalties of up to $500 (first), $750 (second) and $1,000 (subsequent offenses), and the amount wrongfully charged is remitted to the applicant.
rules.key_value: $50 cap (CPI-adjusted annually)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to residential rental properties for dwelling purposes, except one- and two-family dwellings and non-landlord real estate licensees.
rules.exemptions: Exempts units in one- or two-family dwellings offered for rent, and NJ Real Estate Commission licensees unless the licensee is the landlord.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord, or
agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply
to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which
exceeds $50.

rules.title: NJ Fair Chance in Housing Act
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about or consider an applicant's criminal record before making a conditional offer. After a conditional offer, only certain convictions within set look-back periods may be considered, subject to an individualized assessment, written notice of withdrawal, and an appeal opportunity. Providers also may not require drug or alcohol tests of applicants.
rules.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer; look-back 6 years (1st degree), 4 years (2nd/3rd degree), 1 year (4th degree); serious listed offenses and lifetime sex-offender registration have no look-back limit
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers rental dwelling units offered for rent by housing providers, other than units in owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.
rules.exemptions: A dwelling unit in an owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units is not a covered rental dwelling unit.
rules.interaction: Does not bar or affect independent rights or actions, including under the Law Against Discrimination (P.L.1945, c.169). Enforcement is through the Division on Civil Rights rather than court actions.
rules.quoted_span:
A housing
provider
shall not make any oral or written inquiry
regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.

rules.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination source-of-income ban
rules.requirement: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination requires equal treatment in renting housing regardless of listed characteristics, including source of lawful income. A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history.
rules.key_value: Source of lawful income is a protected class
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all landlord-tenant relationships in New Jersey except two-family owner-occupied dwellings and rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home (and certain sex-exclusive or age-restricted housing as it pertains to familial status).
rules.exemptions: Excludes two-family owner-occupied dwellings, rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home, and residences planned exclusively for and occupied by one sex or age-restricted housing as it pertains to familial status.
rules.interaction: A landlord may still refuse to rent for insufficient income or poor credit history under the federal provisions the guide cites (42 U.S.C.A. § 3601 to -3610).
rules.citation: N.J.S.A. 10:5-12; New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)
rules.quoted_span:
prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires 
equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin,

supporting_sources.citation_as_extracted: New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (N.J.S.A. 10:5-1 et seq.)
supporting_sources.quoted_span:
The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination  based
on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent
or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses.

rules.title: NJ FAIR Act algorithmic rent-setting ban
rules.requirement: It is unlawful for rental property owners to pay for or use a coordinator's services, for coordinators to perform a coordinating function or facilitate agreements restricting competition, and for any persons to engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination through algorithmic pricing. Violations are treated as violations of the New Jersey Antitrust Act, and municipalities may not enact conflicting ordinances.
rules.key_value: Bans use or operation of algorithmic rent-setting that pools competitively sensitive information or sets parallel prices
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental property owners (anyone owning one or more residential rental units in NJ), their agents, and coordinators operating algorithmic revenue management software or algorithmic devices.
rules.exemptions: Excludes research/statistical use not used to set rents, free public rent estimates, equal-terms real estate brokerage databases that do not set or recommend rents, and government-set rents under affordability controls; residential dwelling units exclude inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities.
rules.interaction: Supplements and does not limit the New Jersey Antitrust Act (P.L.1970, c.73), whose enforcement provisions in sections 6 through 17 apply to violations. Municipalities cannot enact ordinances conflicting with the act except those explicitly authorized or required by other law. Municipalities may not enact ordinances conflicting with the act, so local algorithm bans in Jersey City and Hoboken may be preempted.
rules.conflict_note: Possible conflict with Jersey City Code § 218-12 (r-0043); needs human review. Possible conflict with Hoboken City Code § 158-2 (Ord. No. B-781) (r-0046); needs human review.

rules.title: Massachusetts prohibition on local rent control
rules.requirement: No Massachusetts city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. A municipality that accepts the chapter may adopt only a voluntary, compensated form of rent control, which cannot cover units of owners with fewer than ten rental units or units with fair market rent above $400.
rules.key_value: Local rent control prohibited; narrow voluntary exception
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to all Massachusetts cities and towns that might adopt local rent control, and thereby to residential rental units statewide.
rules.exemptions: A city or town that accepts the chapter may adopt rent control only if compliance is voluntary after six months, it excludes units owned by persons or entities owning fewer than ten rental units or with fair market rent over $400, it does not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal from regulation, and the municipality compensates owners for the difference between fair market rent and the controlled rent.
rules.interaction: Displaces any local rent control ordinance in Massachusetts cities such as Boston and Cambridge, except the narrow voluntary, compensated form the statute permits. Displaces local rent control in MA; no local rent-cap groups present.

rules.coverage_conditions: Residences generally, with exemptions for several unit types; the article does not give the full coverage terms.
rules.exemptions: Exempted several types of units, including those operated solely for religious purposes; other exemptions are described only as secular and are not specified.
rules.interaction: The article notes supporters may try again on the 2028 ballot or via compromise legislation; no interaction with other laws is stated.

rules.title: Massachusetts security deposit law
rules.requirement: A lessor may not require more than first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit equal to one month's rent, and the cost of a key and lock at or before the start of a tenancy. The deposit must be held in a separate interest-bearing Massachusetts bank account, accrue 5% annual interest (or the lesser bank rate) after one year, and be returned with itemized deductions within 30 days after the tenancy ends.
rules.key_value: Security deposit capped at one month's rent; return within 30 days
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to leases and tenancies of residential real property in Massachusetts.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to a lease, rental, occupancy or tenancy of 100 days or less for vacation or recreational purposes.
rules.interaction: Lease provisions that conflict with the section, and tenant waivers of it, are void as against public policy. A fee in lieu of a deposit may be allowed only through regulations of the executive office of housing and livable communities, in consultation with the attorney general.
rules.quoted_span: (iii) a security deposit equal to the first month's rent provided that such security deposit is deposited as required by subsection (3) and that the tenant is given the statement of condition as required by subsection (2);

rules.title: Massachusetts broker fee rule
rules.requirement: A licensed broker or salesperson may contract solely with the prospective tenant or solely with the landlord, not both. Any broker fee may only be paid by the party (lessor or tenant) who originally engaged and contracted with the broker.
rules.key_value: Fee paid only by the party who hired the broker
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person engaged in finding rental dwelling accommodations for a fee in Massachusetts; the text states no limits by building age or size.
rules.quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.

rules.title: Massachusetts source-of-income discrimination ban
rules.requirement: It is an unlawful practice for any person furnishing rental accommodations to discriminate against an individual because the individual receives federal, state or local public assistance, or is a tenant receiving housing subsidies such as rental assistance or rental supplements, or because of any requirement of such programs.
rules.key_value: No discrimination against public assistance or housing subsidy recipients (including rental assistance)
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person furnishing rental accommodations, with no stated building-based limits in this subsection.
rules.quoted_span: For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements,

rules.title: Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance rent increases
rules.requirement: Landlords of RSO units may raise rent only once every 12 months by the allowable percentage published by LAHD. Rent may be reset to market only in listed circumstances, such as the tenant voluntarily moving out or being evicted for cause.
rules.key_value: Once per 12 months, by the LAHD-published allowable percentage
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental properties first built on or before October 1, 1978 (and replacement units under LAMC 151.28) of the listed types, such as apartments, duplexes, and two or more single-family units on one parcel.
rules.exemptions: Rent is not regulated for condominium and townhome tenancies that commenced after December 31, 1995; landlords may apply for a Luxury Exemption if they can establish the monthly rent charged on or before May 31, 1978.
rules.interaction: Landlords may seek additional increases through LAHD-approved programs (capital improvement, primary renovation, seismic retrofit, rehabilitation, just and reasonable). Properties not covered by the RSO remain subject to the Just Cause Ordinance.
rules.citation: Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (LAMC ch. XV, art. 1)
rules.quoted_span: Rent may be increased once every 12 months by the allowable rent increase percentage

rules.title: Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance
rules.requirement: Landlords may not terminate a covered tenancy without just cause. At-fault reasons include nonpayment, uncured lease violations, nuisance, and illegal use. No-fault reasons, such as owner or family move-in, demolition, or removal from the rental market, generally require relocation assistance to the tenant. Landlords may not evict for unpaid rent unless the amount owed exceeds the Fair Market Rent for the unit's bedroom size, and all eviction notices must be filed with LAHD within three business days of service.
rules.key_value: Relocation assistance for no-fault evictions; no eviction for rent owed below Fair Market Rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Most residential rental properties in the City of Los Angeles that are not covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO), including buildings newer than October 1, 1978 and single-family dwellings, once the tenant has lived in the unit at least six months or the original lease has expired, whichever comes first.
rules.exemptions: Exceptions include transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, an owner's roommate, some cooperatives, some non-profit homeless or short-term substance-abuse treatment facilities, and some HACLA or government-owned properties. Units regulated by the RSO are covered by that ordinance instead.
rules.interaction: The JCO applies to units not regulated by the RSO and does not regulate rent increases; state law AB 1482 may separately regulate rent amounts in buildings older than 15 years.
rules.citation: Los Angeles Just Cause for Eviction Ordinance (JCO)
rules.quoted_span: It prohibits terminations of tenancies without just cause and requires relocation assistance for no-fault evictions.

rules.title: Los Angeles RSO/JCO eviction and relocation assistance
rules.requirement: RSO tenants may be evicted only for listed at-fault reasons (e.g., nonpayment, nuisance, illegal use) or no-fault reasons (e.g., owner move-in, demolition, government order). No-fault evictions require a declaration filed with LAHD, 30- and 60-day written notices, and payment of tenant relocation assistance.
rules.key_value: No-fault evictions require relocation assistance and a filed Landlord Declaration of Intent to Evict
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units subject to the Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance (generally buildings first built on or before October 1, 1978).
rules.interaction: Notices to terminate a tenancy for RSO units must be filed with LAHD within three business days of service. Properties not covered by the RSO remain subject to the city's Just Cause Ordinance. Demolition for new construction is governed instead by the Resident Protections Ordinance.

rules.title: Los Angeles Resident Protections Ordinance
rules.requirement: When a Protected Unit is demolished for new construction, the owner must pay relocation under State Housing Crisis Act or City law, whichever is higher, with enhanced standardized payments for lower-income households, plus rights to remain up to 6 months, return, and first refusal.
rules.key_value: Standardized payment (Chart B): $115,480 extremely low / $96,750 very low / $87,450 low income
rules.coverage_conditions: Protected Units (including all RSO units and units recently rent-restricted or occupied by lower-income households) that will be demolished for new construction; enhanced payments apply to lower-income households.
rules.interaction: Codifies and expands the State Housing Crisis Act protections; owner must pay the highest applicable amount under State and City law. Above-low-income households receive RSO/JCO Chart A amounts. Codifies State Housing Crisis Act protections.

rules.requirement: Council is asked to instruct the Los Angeles Housing Department to report on how many ownership and management entities use algorithm-based software to set rents and on the feasibility of banning such software in the City. No ban has been adopted by this motion.
rules.coverage_conditions: No coverage is defined; the motion only requests a study of algorithm-based rent-setting software use in the City.
rules.interaction: The motion notes that San Francisco approved legislation in July 2024 banning algorithm-based rent-setting tools, but does not state how any Los Angeles measure would interact with other laws.

rules.title: San Francisco annual allowable rent increase
rules.requirement: For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable rent increase effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6% of the tenant's base rent.

rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rent-controlled units in San Francisco; the page does not define which units qualify.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause and relocation
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict a tenant from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for one of 17 listed just cause reasons, which must be the dominant motive for the eviction. Expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership is not just cause.
rules.key_value: 17 just cause reasons (Ordinance § 37.9(a))
rules.coverage_conditions: Rental units covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance, including some units exempt from the rent increase limits (such as units first receiving a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies, and some tenancies regulated by another agency).
rules.exemptions: The page does not list exemptions from the eviction provisions; it states that some tenancies exempt from the rent increase limits remain subject to just cause eviction rules.
rules.interaction: Tenancies exempt from the Ordinance's rent increase limits (post-June 13, 1979 construction, Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies, some government-regulated rents) are still subject to the just cause eviction provisions. Ellis Act withdrawals are recognized as one just cause reason.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.

rules.title: San Francisco Fair Chance Ordinance
rules.requirement: San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance protects residents with arrest or conviction history in affordable housing decisions. The page gives no further detail on specific limits or procedures.

rules.quoted_span: San Francisco's Fair Chance Ordinance protects residents with arrest or conviction history in affordable housing decisions.

rules.title: San Francisco ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to sell or use algorithmic devices, such as software that analyzes nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend what rent to charge for a vacant unit, to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units. A tenant or the City Attorney may bring a civil action over a violation.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale or use of algorithmic rent-setting devices
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
rules.quoted_span: The law prohibits the sale or use of such algorithmic devices and allows a tenant or the City Attorney to bring a civil action if they believe an entity is in violation of the law.

supporting_sources.quoted_span: The ordinance prohibits landlords from using qualifying algorithmic devices that calculate nonpublic competitor information to advise on rent or occupancy.

rules.title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protection Ordinance
rules.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a tenancy without just cause, either at-fault (e.g., nonpayment, material lease breach, nuisance) or no-fault (e.g., owner move-in, withdrawal from market, government order, demolition or substantial remodel). For no-fault terminations the landlord must pay relocation assistance of two months' rent (three months for seniors or disabled tenants) or waive an equal amount of rent, and give 30 or 60 days' written notice.
rules.key_value: No-fault relocation: 2 months' rent (3 months if tenant is senior or disabled)
rules.coverage_conditions: Covers residential rental tenancies of more than 30 days in San Diego, except housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years and other listed exempt housing types.
rules.exemptions: Exempt: certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years; owner-occupied single-family homes and owner-occupied duplexes; separately alienable property owned by a non-corporate landlord with written exemption notice; deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing (not Section 8); hotels, short-term rentals, mobilehomes, institutional housing, dormitories, and shared-facility rentals with a resident landlord.
rules.interaction: The ordinance implements and is consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2, and the rights it confers are in addition to existing state and federal rights. Relocation assistance paid under this Division is credited against any other relocation assistance required by federal, state, or other local law.
rules.quoted_span:
A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause. For purposes of this 
Division, just cause includes at-fault just cause and no-fault just cause.

supporting_sources.citation_as_extracted: San Diego Municipal Code ch. 9, art. 8, div. 7 (§§ 98.0701 et seq.)
supporting_sources.quoted_span: The purpose of the Ordinance is to require Just Cause for termination of residential tenancies consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2,

rules.title: San Diego ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices
rules.requirement: It would be unlawful to sell, license or otherwise provide an algorithmic rent-setting device (software using nonpublic competitor data to recommend rents or occupancy levels) to a landlord, and unlawful for a landlord to use one to set rents or occupancy levels. Tenants may sue for injunctive relief, damages or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees; each month and each property is a separate violation.

rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to any person selling or providing algorithmic devices to landlords and to landlords setting rents or occupancy levels for residential rental property in the City of San Diego.
rules.exemptions: The definition of 'algorithmic device' excludes software that only publishes reports from aggregated historical nonpublic data more than 90 days old or from public information without recommending future rents, and software used to set rents or income limits under local, state or federal affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.interaction: Remedies are cumulative with other remedies in the Division or at law, statute or ordinance; the document names no preemption or yielding relationship.
rules.quoted_span:
It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates
or occupancy levels for residential rental property.

rules.title: Berkeley rent stabilization and annual general adjustment
rules.requirement: Landlords of fully covered units may raise rent each year only by the Annual General Adjustment set by the Rent Board using a CPI-based formula, and Measure BB caps the AGA at 5% even if the formula yields more. Landlords with banked AGAs may still raise rent above 5% to reach the rent ceiling.
rules.key_value: CPI-based AGA, max 5%
rules.coverage_conditions: Fully covered units: most units in multifamily properties built before 1980, certain older single-family homes with pre-1996 tenancies, single-family homes with five or more rooms rented individually, and government-subsidized units that are fully covered; rent ceilings apply to these units.
rules.exemptions: Partially covered units (new construction with certificate of occupancy after 1980, most single-family homes and condominiums, and units whose subsidies are exempt from rent control under federal or state law) are not subject to the rent ceiling.
rules.interaction: The cap does not prevent landlords with banked AGAs from raising rent above 5% to reach the rent ceiling. Costa-Hawkins removes certain tenancies from the adjustment but no group for it exists.
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance (Measure BB); Berkeley Municipal Code § 13.76.110(A)
rules.quoted_span: The maximum AGA is 5%. This means that, if the formula in the Rent Ordinance results in an AGA that is greater than 5%, the AGA approved by the Board for that year can be no more than 5%.

rules.title: Berkeley relocation assistance for owner move-in and Ellis Act evictions
rules.requirement: Owners must pay tenants relocation assistance when evicting for an owner move-in or to withdraw a unit from the rental market under the Ellis Act. The payment amounts are indexed to inflation and adjusted each year by the Rent Board.
rules.key_value: Standard payment $19,413; additional payment for qualifying households $6,471 (effective 2026-01-01; 1.5% CPI adjustment)
rules.coverage_conditions: Tenants evicted for an owner move-in or for removal of the property from the rental market under the Ellis Act; the page does not state further coverage tests.
rules.interaction: The Ellis Implementation Ordinance requires the same relocation payments as the Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance; both index the amounts to inflation. Ellis ordinance requires the same relocation payments as the Rent Stabilization Ordinance.

rules.quoted_span: The Rent Stabilization and Good Cause for Eviction Ordinance requires owners to pay tenants relocation assistance in the event of an owner move-in eviction.

rules.title: Berkeley just cause for eviction
rules.requirement: Tenants in fully or partially covered units cannot be evicted without just cause. Measure BB bars eviction for rental debt under one month of Fair Market Rent or for refusing to sign a new fixed-term lease, requires lease-breach evictions to show substantial actual harm and unreasonable tenant behavior, and requires notices to be filed with the Rent Board within three business days.
rules.key_value: Nonpayment eviction only if debt >= one month's Fair Market Rent
rules.coverage_conditions: Units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance, including government-owned or -subsidized units now required to register.
rules.exemptions: Units exempt from the Rent Ordinance, such as shared kitchen/bath units where the landlord lived on the property before the tenant, are not covered.
rules.citation: Berkeley Rent Stabilization Ordinance (as amended by Measure BB)
rules.quoted_span: In Berkeley, tenants in units that are fully or partially covered by the Rent Ordinance cannot be evicted unless there is "just cause” (previously called “good cause”).

rules.title: Berkeley security deposit interest requirement
rules.requirement: For tenancies in units fully or partially covered by the Berkeley Rent Ordinance, landlords must pay tenants interest on the security deposit at the end of each year, and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before year end.
rules.key_value: Annual interest on deposit, prorated on move-out
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to tenancies in units fully or partially covered by Berkeley's Rent Ordinance.
rules.interaction: Operates alongside the California state security deposit rules described on the same page. Operates alongside state deposit rules.
rules.quoted_span: landlords must pay tenants interest on their security deposit at the end of each year and a prorated amount if the tenant moves out before the end of the year.

rules.title: Berkeley screening fee disclosure ordinance
rules.requirement: Owners charging a fee for a credit report or application processing must provide a clear tenant screening fee rights statement and the state maximum fee cap before receiving the fee. Owners may not charge existing tenants a non-refundable fee for renewing a tenancy or for adding, replacing, or removing a roommate.

rules.title: Berkeley Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Rental housing providers may not ask about or use criminal history in advertising, applications, tenant selection, or tenancy decisions, and must give written notice and an opportunity to respond before taking any action based on criminal history. Violations carry administrative fines of $1,000 to $10,000 per violation plus civil damages.
rules.key_value: Criminal history inquiries and use prohibited; fines $1,000-$10,000 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rental housing providers in Berkeley with respect to current and prospective tenants, unless an exemption applies.
rules.exemptions: Exempt: lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing/Section 8 properties; owner-occupied 1-3 unit properties where an owner lives in one unit; units under an owner move-back rental agreement (BMC 13.76.130 A.9); existing tenants subletting or adding/replacing roommates.
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.

rules.title: Berkeley ban on coordinated rent-pricing algorithms
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license, or provide to Berkeley landlords, or for a landlord to use, a coordinated pricing algorithm that uses non-public competitor data to set or recommend rents or occupancy levels for residential units. Each month and each unit constitutes a separate violation, with civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation plus attorney's fees.
rules.key_value: Ban on coordinated pricing algorithms; civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation
rules.coverage_conditions: All landlords of residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley, and vendors who sell or license coordinated pricing algorithms to them.
rules.exemptions: The definition of coordinated pricing algorithm excludes aggregated anonymous rental data reports, products used to set affordable housing rent or income limits, and products used for market research for project financing, appraisals, or software research, testing, and training.
rules.quoted_span:
It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described 
in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in 
the City of Berkeley.

rules.title: Santa Ana rent stabilization annual cap
rules.requirement: Residential rent increases are limited to the lower of 3% per year or 80% of the 12-month percent change in the CPI; if the CPI is negative, no increase is permitted. Owners may petition for a higher increase by showing it is needed for a fair and reasonable return.
rules.key_value: lower of 3% or 80% of CPI change per year; no increase if CPI negative
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental buildings in Santa Ana constructed on or before February 1, 1995, plus mobile home spaces offered for rent on or before January 1, 1990.
rules.exemptions: Residential buildings constructed after February 1, 1995 and mobile home spaces offered for rent after January 1, 1990 are not subject to the cap.
rules.quoted_span: Increase in residential rents are limited to the lower of 3% per year, or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period.

rules.title: Santa Ana just cause eviction
rules.requirement: After 30 days of tenancy, an owner may not terminate a tenancy without just cause stated in a written notice, and must first give notice and an opportunity to cure for at-fault causes. rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental properties in Santa Ana, except housing produced in the last 15 years and the other excluded property types.
rules.exemptions: Housing produced in the last 15 years; deed-restricted affordable housing; hotel and transient occupancy; hospital and care facilities; dormitories; and other shared living quarters.
rules.citation: Santa Ana Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
rules.quoted_span: After 30 days, an owner shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in a written notice.

rules.title: Hoboken rent control
rules.requirement: Rents in covered dwellings are controlled at the base rent received on October 1, 1985. At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not raise rent by more than the lesser of 5% or the CPI change. Only one cost-of-living increase is permitted in any twelve-month period, increases require 30 days' written notice, and increases beyond those allowed are void and refundable. Separate board-approved surcharges (taxes, water/sewer, capital improvements) and hardship increases are also available.
rules.key_value: Lesser of 5% or CPI change; one increase per 12 months
rules.coverage_conditions: All dwelling units (buildings or structures rented or offered for rent to one or more tenants) in Hoboken, other than the listed exemptions.
rules.exemptions: Exempt: motels/hotels; first rental of newly constructed dwellings; industrial and commercial property; school-controlled student housing; government-owned housing; buildings vacant since 1/1/1984 (first rental only); multiple dwellings built after 6/25/1987 for a limited period under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.1; units under preempting government-agency rent regulation during that period.
rules.interaction: Exemption for post-1987 multiple dwellings applies in accordance with N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.1 et seq. The chapter is preempted while a governmental agency's rent regulation superseding the City's authority is in effect.
rules.quoted_span: no landlord may request or receive a percentage increase in rent which is greater than 5% or the percentage difference between the consumer price index three months prior to the expiration or termination of the lease and three months prior to the commencement of the lease term, whichever is less.

supporting_sources.quoted_span: said rental shall be limited to an increase of 25% over the last rental paid by the tenant who voluntarily vacated the rental unit, exclusive of any capital improvement surcharge that is a component of said last rental.

rules.title: Hoboken large rent increase disclosures
rules.requirement: Residential landlords seeking to raise rent by more than 10% year over year on renewal must give the tenant an itemization of costs, a statement on whether a rent algorithm was used, notice of the right to take legal action, and Division of Housing contact information. Failure to disclose is punishable by a fine of up to $1,000 per incident.
rules.key_value: Disclosures required for increases >10%; fine up to $1,000 per incident
rules.coverage_conditions: All residential landlords in Hoboken who raise rent by more than 10% year over year on renewal of a lease with a current tenant.

rules.title: Hoboken prohibition on algorithmic rent fixing
rules.requirement: Landlords of residential units in Hoboken may not use software, algorithms or data-sharing platforms to collect and analyze nonpublic competitor information in order to coordinate, recommend or implement rents, lease terms or occupancy levels among competing lessors. Violations are enforced in Municipal Court by the Division of Housing or an aggrieved private citizen, with penalties of up to a $2,000 fine and/or up to 90 days community service, or penalties under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5.
rules.key_value: Ban on algorithmic pricing using nonpublic competitor data; fine up to $2,000 or up to 90 days community service
rules.coverage_conditions: All landlords renting a residential dwelling unit (any primary residence) in Hoboken.
rules.exemptions: Medical/long-term care facilities and detention facilities are excluded from the definition of residential dwelling unit.
rules.interaction: Penalties may be imposed as prescribed under N.J.S.A. 40:49-5.
rules.quoted_span: Landlords who rent any residential dwelling unit (defined as any primary residence excluding medical/long-term care or detention facilities) in the City of Hoboken are prohibited from price fixing using algorithmic pricing.
rules.conflict_note: Possible conflict with P.L. 2026, c.43 (C.56:9-20 to 56:9-26) (r-0013); needs human review.

rules.title: Newark Rent Control Ordinance
rules.requirement: At lease expiration or termination of a periodic tenancy, a landlord may not request or receive an increase greater than the CPI percentage change (CPI-U NY-NJ-Long Island, from 15 months prior to 3 months prior to the month of the proposed increase), and in no case more than 4%. Increases are barred if the dwelling is not in substantial compliance or the landlord has not registered, and require 30 days' written notice to the tenant and the Rent Regulation Officer.
rules.key_value: CPI-U change, max 4%
rules.coverage_conditions: All multiple dwellings, as defined in the chapter (any building or structure containing one or more apartments rented or offered to one or more tenants), are subject to rent control.
rules.exemptions: Exempt dwellings include public housing, hotel/motel space rented day-to-day to transients, commercial space, newly constructed multiple dwellings and vacant dwellings (per \u00a7\u00a7 19:2-18.1 and 18.2, not in this part), certain rehabilitated units receiving Section 8 or Rental Rehabilitation subsidies, and units under a preemptive governmental agency rent-regulation contract.
rules.interaction: The base increase may be supplemented by Board-approved tax surcharges, major new improvement surcharges and hardship increases, all conditioned on substantial compliance and registration; an owner-occupied definition (four units or less with the owner residing in one) appears in the chapter, though its effect is not stated in this part.
rules.quoted_span: no landlord may request or receive an increase greater than the percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the CPI 15 months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase to the CPI three months prior to the month of the proposed rent increase. In no case shall the allowable rent increase exceed 4%.

the Rent Control Board shall not grant increases exceeding 25% in any one year for any tenant.

rules.title: Newark HOME-assisted unit maximum rents
rules.requirement: Rents for HOME-assisted units in Newark's Neighborhood Rehabilitation Program may not exceed the lesser of HUD fair market rent or the rent affordable to a family at 65% of area median income (30% of adjusted income), minus utility allowances where the tenant pays utilities. Owners must give tenants at least 30 days' prior written notice of any rent increase, and leases must be for at least one year unless mutually agreed otherwise.
rules.key_value: Lesser of HUD fair market rent or 30% of adjusted income at 65% of area median income; 30 days' written notice of increase
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies only to rental units assisted with HOME funds through the City's Neighborhood Rehabilitation Program (owner-occupied structures of one to three dwelling units), for the applicable affordability period (5, 10 or 15 years depending on funds awarded).
rules.exemptions: Mixed use or nonresidential buildings are not eligible for the program.
rules.interaction: HOME rent limits are set by HUD and recalculated periodically; any rent increase remains subject to the terms of outstanding leases, and tax-credit units follow IRC section 42 rent rules.
rules.quoted_span: Any increase in rents for HOME assisted units is subject to the provisions of outstanding leases, and in any event, the owner must provide tenants of those units not less than 30 days prior written notice before implementing any increase in rents.

rules.title: Newark unconscionable rent increase ordinance
rules.requirement: Newark defines an 'unconscionable rent' increase for residential rental properties as one that is exceedingly harsh or unreasonable, exceeds the increase in the landlord's expenses, and is not comparable to rents at similar properties. For properties under a redevelopment or financial agreement, rent above the approved pro-forma is per se unconscionable.
rules.key_value: Rent above approved pro-forma is per se unconscionable
rules.coverage_conditions: Residential rental properties in Newark, including market-rate and unsubsidized units, other than statutorily exempt or HUD-controlled units.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to units statutorily exempt from rent control under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.1 to 84.6 or units controlled and governed by HUD.
rules.interaction: The definition carves out units exempt from rent control under N.J.S.A. 2A:42-84.1-84.6 and HUD-controlled units; the operative prohibition and remedies are not in this part of the document.
rules.quoted_span: Shall mean any rental increase for residential properties including but not limited to market and unsubsidized units, whose rental increases are exceedingly harsh or unreasonable that exceed the increase in the landlord’s expenses; and is not comparable to rents charged at similar properties.

rules.title: Newark retaliatory eviction prohibition
rules.requirement: A landlord may not bring an action to recover possession of a dwelling unit as a reprisal for the tenant's efforts to secure or enforce any right under the rent control chapter.
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to dwelling units subject to the Newark rent control chapter; no further coverage tests are stated in this part.
rules.interaction: The ordinance elsewhere references the state Anti-Eviction Act (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 et seq.) and the Senior Citizens and Disabled Protected Tenancy Act (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.22) in connection with unlawful entry and condominium conversion protections.
rules.quoted_span: No landlord shall bring any action to recover possession of a dwelling unit as a reprisal for the tenant's efforts to secure or enforce any right under this chapter.

rules.title: Newark Ban the Box rental screening
rules.requirement: Landlords and brokers may inquire into criminal history only after a formal application and written notice and consent, may look back only 8 years for indictable convictions and 5 years for disorderly persons/ordinance convictions (certain serious offenses at any time), may not use non-pending arrests, expunged/sealed records or juvenile adjudications, must weigh rehabilitation factors, and must give written reasons and the results within 10 business days of an adverse decision.
rules.key_value: Lookback: 8 years (indictable), 5 years (disorderly persons/ordinance); after formal application only
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to rentals, leases and subleases of real property in Newark by landlords and real estate brokers, except certain owner-occupied small dwellings.
rules.exemptions: Does not apply to a single apartment in an owner-occupied two-family dwelling or a room rental in an owner-occupied one-family dwelling; also does not apply where federal or state law requires or permits criminal-history consideration (limited to those offenses and periods) or to property in government programs encouraging housing for people with criminal histories.
rules.interaction: Prohibitions do not apply where federal or state law, regulation or rule requires or permits consideration of criminal history, limited to the offenses and time periods that law allows.
rules.quoted_span: Inquiry into and consideration of any applicant's criminal history shall take place only after the applicant has submitted a formal application.

rules.title: Boston Housing Stability Notification Act
rules.requirement: A landlord or foreclosing owner ending a tenancy must deliver a Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources to the tenant at the same time as the Notice to Quit or non-renewal notice, and send a copy of that notice with a Certificate of Compliance/Service to the City's Office of Housing Stability. Violations draw a warning, then $300 per day, but do not halt the eviction process.
rules.key_value: Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources delivered with Notice to Quit; copy to Office of Housing Stability
rules.coverage_conditions: All landlords and foreclosing owners intending to end a tenancy or post-foreclosure occupancy of a unit in the City of Boston.
rules.exemptions: Only residences in hospitals, skilled nursing or health facilities, and non-profit short-term substance abuse treatment facilities are exempt.
rules.interaction: The requirements cannot be waived by lease or contract; violation does not halt the eviction process.
rules.quoted_span: The HSNA becomes effective on November 6, 2020.

rules.requirement: Covered housing providers may not impose blanket denials based on arrests or convictions and must not consider non-conviction arrests, judicially relieved convictions, juvenile records, or convictions more than 5 years old (subject to exceptions for direct relationship/unreasonable risk of harm). They also may not use applicants' credit scores to approve or deny applications.
rules.key_value: No blanket bans; no consideration of arrests without conviction, sealed/expunged or juvenile records, or convictions over 5 years old; no credit score use
rules.coverage_conditions: Housing providers receiving DND funding and/or land, or with income-restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy (also applied to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program).
rules.exemptions: Criminal-history limits do not apply where there is a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought and/or unreasonable risk of substantial harm to others, or to current criminal behavior.
rules.interaction: Where federal or state law imposes a criminal history requirement that conflicts with this guidance, the federal or state law preempts the policy. Federal or state criminal-history requirements preempt the policy, but no corresponding groups exist.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (DND, Feb. 2017)
rules.quoted_span:
will not impose a blanket policy that denies 
housing to anyone with arrests and or convictions. Housing providers will consider applicants on 
a case-by-case basis.

rules.title: Boston rental assistance discrimination ban
rules.requirement: Landlords in Boston may not discriminate against tenants or applicants because they use rental assistance, including Section 8 vouchers, social security disability vouchers and veterans vouchers. Telling an applicant the landlord does not accept rental assistance is cited as an example of housing discrimination.
rules.key_value: Rental assistance is a protected class
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to renting, buying, selling or securing financing for any housing in the City of Boston; no further coverage tests are stated.
rules.interaction: The page says the commission enforces local, state and federal fair housing laws, but it does not say how this rule interacts with any specific law.
rules.citation: Boston Fair Housing Commission fair housing regulations
rules.quoted_span:
The landlord tells you they don't accept rental assistance. This includes Section
8 vouchers, social security disability vouchers, and veterans vouchers.

rules.title: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Source of income, including Section 8 and public benefits, is a protected category under the Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance, so landlords cannot discriminate against applicants on that basis. Landlords and rental agents may use any reasonable tenant selection standard (such as ability to pay rent and to care for the apartment) if it is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.
rules.key_value: Source of income (incl. Section 8 and public benefits) is a protected category
rules.coverage_conditions: Applies to housing transactions in Cambridge, including viewing or renting an apartment and terms and conditions of tenancy, with no building age or size tests stated.
rules.exemptions: Exemption for 2-family dwellings when the owner lives there.
rules.quoted_span: Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.
